Petrarch, letter from Parma, 1349: 'Will posterity believe' that the earth was emptied without war or flood?
Plague hit China in the early 1330s before reaching the Black Sea and Italy in 1347.
A popular claim says 'Ring a Ring o' Roses' describes the plague. Folklorists reject this. The rhyme is first printed in 1881 and the plague link appears only in the 20th century.

Futurists agree the Black Death did not fulfil the end-time prophecies. They hold the true fulfilment is still ahead, perhaps in the seal judgments (Revelation 6:8). Historicists have often placed great medieval plagues within the trumpet and bowl visions. Idealists see such events as typical of the whole age.
Are modern epidemics such as AIDS or COVID-19 worse than past plagues, and so signs of the last days?
In share of population, no. Modern epidemics are tragic, but the Black Death killed a far larger part of humanity. Size alone does not make an event prophetic.

This reading compares by proportion, not by headlines. When the Black Death struck, world population was perhaps 400 to 500 million. Scholars suggest 75 million or more died, around one person in six worldwide. AIDS has killed about 42 million people since 1981, out of a world population of 5 to 8 billion. That is a little over half of one percent. COVID-19 had about 7 million reported deaths by 2024, with estimates of excess deaths much higher. Each death is a real loss. But the numbers show our age is not unique. On this reading, even such comparisons are beside the point. The signs of Matthew 24 were limited by Jesus' time text to the generation before AD 70.
Black Death: perhaps 75 to 200 million dead worldwide, out of roughly 450 million people.
AIDS: about 42 million deaths from 1981 to 2023 (UNAIDS estimates).
The 1918 influenza killed perhaps 50 million out of about 1.8 billion people.

Some futurist teachers say the key sign is not size but the combination of many signs at once, together with Israel's return and global technology. Others link pandemics to the fourth seal of Revelation 6:8. Many Christians of every view simply see disease as part of the curse that Christ will finally remove (Revelation 21:4).
Are earthquakes really increasing in our time, as some prophecy writers claim?
No good evidence shows it. Seismologists say the number of large earthquakes is fairly steady. We simply detect and report far more of them.

In 1980 Hal Lindsey wrote that the number of earthquakes per decade had roughly doubled since 1950. He gave no data. The United States Geological Survey says the rate of magnitude 7 or larger earthquakes has stayed fairly constant over the last century. More quakes are recorded because there are many more seismograph stations and faster global news. In the early 1900s the French scholar Count Montessus de Ballore catalogued about 171,000 earthquakes from recorded history. Great killers came long before our day. The Shaanxi earthquake of 1556 killed perhaps 830,000. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus spoke of earthquakes 'in various places' before AD 70, and his time text limits that sign.
Lisbon, 1 November 1755 (All Saints' Day): earthquake, tsunami and fire. Estimates range from 30,000 to 50,000 or more deaths.
Shaanxi, China, 1556: the deadliest recorded earthquake.
USGS: about 15 earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more occur per year on average, with no long-term rise.

Some futurists now grant that frequency is not rising. They say the sign is the overall 'birth pains' pattern, or that quake deaths and damage are rising because of crowded cities. Others look to a future great earthquake (Revelation 16:18). Few careful scholars of any view now rely on frequency statistics.
Were there earthquakes in the first century to fulfil Jesus' words before AD 70?
Yes. Ancient writers report many. Seneca, who died in AD 65, spoke of whole cities destroyed by earthquakes in Asia, Achaia, Syria and Macedonia.

On the fulfilled reading, Jesus' sign of earthquakes 'in various places' (Matthew 24:7) was met in the years AD 30-70. The New Testament records an earthquake at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:51), at the resurrection (Matthew 28:2), and at Philippi (Acts 16:26). Roman sources add more. Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). Pompeii was badly damaged in AD 62 or 63 (Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1). Seneca also wrote of how often cities in Asia and Achaia had been laid low, and of Paphos on Cyprus collapsing. He wrote this only a few years before Jerusalem fell. So the disciples did not need to wait centuries to see this sign.
Tacitus, Annals 14.27: Laodicea rebuilt itself from its own resources after the AD 60 quake.
Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1: the Campanian (Pompeii) earthquake.
Josephus, Jewish War 4.4.5: a violent storm and earthquake at Jerusalem in AD 68 seemed to men a sign of disaster.

Futurists agree such quakes happened but say they were only the 'beginning of birth pains' (Matthew 24:8). The full sign is still future, with a great global earthquake (Revelation 16:18). Some partial preterists apply the earthquake sign to AD 70 and the bowl judgments to a later time.
How could 'wars and rumors of wars' be a sign during the Roman peace?
Because the Pax Romana made war unusual. When revolts and civil war broke out in the 60s, they stood out. In AD 68-69 Rome itself almost fell.

On the fulfilled reading, the sign makes sense because it came in a time of general peace. Under the Roman peace, large wars were rare. So reports of war were noticed. In the 60s, unrest grew. Britain rebelled under Boudica (AD 60-61). Judea revolted in AD 66. After Nero died in June 68, civil war broke out. Four emperors ruled in about a year: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian. Tacitus called it a year that was almost the last for the state (Histories 1.11). Jesus told his disciples not to be alarmed, because 'the end is not yet' (Matthew 24:6). His time text (24:34) places these wars before AD 70. In an age of constant war, wars would not be much of a sign.
Tacitus, Histories 1.2: a period 'rich in disasters, frightful with battles, torn by civil strife'.
AD 69: the Capitol in Rome burned during fighting between Vitellius's and Vespasian's men.
Josephus, Jewish War 4.9.2: news of Rome's civil war reached Vespasian in Judea.

Futurists say the sign is war on a world scale, nation against kingdom, and see this in the World Wars. Some say the wars of the first century were a partial or near fulfilment. Others, like many amillennialists, see wars as marks of the entire age between Christ's comings.
Are the wars of the last century so terrible that they must be a prelude to the end?
Not on the historical record. Earlier wars killed huge shares of their populations. Each age has thought its wars were the last.

This reading compares the 20th century with earlier ones. World War II was terribly destructive. Perhaps 70 to 85 million died, and atomic bombs were used. But earlier wars were also catastrophic. The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) may have killed a fifth to a third of the German population. The Manchu conquest of China in the 1600s and the Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864) each killed tens of millions. The Paraguayan War (1864-1870) killed perhaps half or more of Paraguay's people. After the Goths defeated Rome at Adrianople in 378, Ambrose of Milan linked them with Ezekiel's Gog and felt the end had come. The key, on this reading, is that Jesus' wars were limited to forty years after his death. With so many wars in history, the sign would mean nothing without a time limit.
Battle of Adrianople, AD 378: Emperor Valens killed. Ambrose (On the Faith 2.16) identified the Goths with Gog.
Taiping Rebellion, 1850-1864: estimates of 20 to 30 million deaths.
Napoleonic Wars, 1803-1815: perhaps 3.5 to 6 million deaths.

Futurists answer that modern war is unique in being truly global and in having weapons that can end human life, as Matthew 24:22 might suggest ('no flesh would be saved'). Others note that the share of people dying in war has fallen since 1945. Amillennialists see wars in every age as part of the 'birth pains'.
If these signs are fulfilled, what should Christians do when disasters happen today?
Repent, pray, help the suffering and keep working. Fulfilled prophecy still teaches lessons that apply to every age.

On this reading, past fulfilment does not make the Bible silent about today. It changes what we do with the news. Instead of building charts, Christians should do what Jesus commanded. He told his hearers to repent when they heard of disaster (Luke 13:5). The early church sent famine relief to Judea (Acts 11:28-30). Paul told believers to do good to all people (Galatians 6:10). God still rules over nations and nature (Psalms 46:1-3). Disasters remind us that creation groans and waits for redemption (Romans 8:22). They also show how short life is (James 4:14). So the right response is faith, love and good works, not fear or date-setting.
Acts 11:28-30: Agabus foretold a famine; the disciples sent help to Judea.
During the Plague of Cyprian (AD 250s), Christians in Carthage cared for the sick of every faith (Pontius, Life of Cyprian 9).
Martin Luther's letter 'Whether One May Flee from a Deadly Plague' (1527) urged care for neighbours.

Christians of every view largely agree on this practical response. Futurists add that today's signs should also stir urgency in evangelism, because the Lord's coming may be very near. Some warn that a fully past reading could weaken watchfulness. Fulfilled readers reply that Christ's final coming is still future and still calls us to watch.
Have confident predictions about Russia and Bible prophecy come true?
No. Writers in 1916, 1928, 1948, 1980 and 1991 said Russia would soon invade Israel. Each forecast passed without fulfilment.

This reading asks readers to notice the dates. In 1916 Arno Gaebelein wrote that Russia's millions would soon be thrown into Palestine. A 1928 Pentecostal article said the conflict would come 'very shortly'. In 1948 a magazine said World War III might start in ninety days. In 1980 Hal Lindsey said the Soviets would use Afghanistan as a springboard to seize Iran. Instead, the Soviet Union left Afghanistan in 1989 and broke apart in 1991. In January 1991 a newsletter said Russia would attack Israel and Europe. The same writer later admitted he had 'jumped the gun'. Scripture gives a test for prophets: if the word does not come true, the LORD did not speak it (Deuteronomy 18:22). Christians should not build their lives on such guesses.
Soviet troops left Afghanistan in February 1989. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
Russia did not take part in the 1991 Gulf War, but the Soviet Union backed the UN resolutions against Iraq.
Dwight Wilson's 'Armageddon Now!' (1977) collects decades of such Russia forecasts.

Many futurist teachers agree that date-setting is wrong and that some predictions were careless. But they hold that the core teaching, a northern coalition attacking Israel in the last days, remains true even if timing guesses failed. They point to Russia's alliances with Iran and its role in Syria since 2015 as fresh signs.
Are many prophecy 'predictions' just current trends read back into the Bible?
On this reading, yes. Writers take what is already happening in politics, project it forward, and then find verses to support it.

This reading argues that much prophecy writing begins with the newspaper, not the text. A writer sees a trend, such as European unity or a Russian arms build-up. He forecasts that it will continue. Then he looks for a verse that seems to fit. When the trend changes, the book is revised. The prophets, by contrast, did not take their message from the news of their day. Peter says prophecy never came by human will. Holy men spoke from God as the Spirit carried them along (2 Peter 1:20-21). Jeremiah condemned prophets who spoke visions from their own minds (Jeremiah 23:16). Prophecy must be read in its own words, time and setting first.
George Orwell noted that political forecasters usually predict 'a continuation of the thing that is happening'.
In the 1970s many books tied prophecy to oil and the Arab world. In the 1990s, to the New World Order. In the 2000s, to terrorism.
2 Peter 1:20-21: no prophecy comes from the prophet's own interpretation.

Futurists answer that Jesus told us to read 'the signs of the times' (Matthew 16:3) and to watch. They say comparing news with Scripture is obedient watchfulness, as long as one avoids dates. Some admit past excesses but say real fulfilments, such as Israel's rebirth, show the method works.
Did the prophets describe modern weapons with ancient words because they could not imagine tanks and missiles?
This reading says no. The prophets spoke from God, and God can describe any weapon. If they spoke of swords and bows, they meant a war fought with swords and bows.

Some writers say a prophet 'could not describe' machine guns, so he wrote of bows and arrows instead. The fulfilled reading replies that modern weapons were not beyond God's imagination. Prophets did not speak from their own understanding but from God (2 Peter 1:21). Ezekiel names horses, swords, shields, bows, arrows, clubs and spears (Ezekiel 38:4; 39:9). He says Israel would burn the wooden weapons for seven years (39:9-10). The simplest reading is that the prophet described a war of his own world. That war lay in his future but is in our past. Futurists cannot have it both ways. They cannot claim a literal reading while turning swords into missiles.
Ezekiel 39:9-10: the people will make fires of the weapons and need no wood from the field.
Daniel 11 describes horses, chariots and ships in wars of the Persian and Greek periods (Daniel 11:40).
Some writers have read Ezekiel's horses as 'horsepower' in engines.

Some futurists hold that the battle will literally use primitive weapons, perhaps after a global collapse. Others say the prophet used the words of his time for weapons he saw in vision, as John may describe helicopters as locusts. Others read Ezekiel 38-39 as symbolic or apocalyptic, so weapons are not the point.
Does 2 Peter 3:10 describe a nuclear war?
This reading says no. Peter used Old Testament judgment language. Reading his words as atomic physics adds modern ideas the text does not contain.

Some writers say Peter's elements melting with fervent heat is a precise description of a nuclear blast. But this is the same writer group that says Ezekiel could not describe modern weapons. Both cannot be true. Peter uses the fire language of the prophets. God's judgments on Sodom, on Edom and on Jerusalem are described with fire and melting (Isaiah 34:4; Micah 1:4; Zephaniah 1:18). The Greek word stoicheia ('elements') can mean basic parts of a system, as in Galatians 4:3, 9 and Colossians 2:8. On the fulfilled or covenantal reading, Peter speaks of the passing of the old covenant world. Other readers see the final renewal of creation. Neither reading needs nuclear physics.
Micah 1:4: mountains melt like wax before the fire. This describes God's judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem.
Galatians 4:3, 9 uses stoicheia for the 'elementary principles' of the old order.
Hiroshima, 6 August 1945, often cited by mid-century writers as a picture of 2 Peter 3.

Most futurist and amillennial scholars also reject a nuclear reading. They see 2 Peter 3 as God's direct final judgment and renewal of the cosmos at Christ's return, not a human war. Some popular writers still see nuclear weapons as one way such fire could come. Full and partial preterists differ on whether 2 Peter 3 is past or future.
Was Saddam Hussein's Iraq a fulfilment of Isaiah 13 and the fall of Babylon?
On this reading, no. Isaiah said Babylon's day was near and named the Medes as God's instrument. That judgment came in Isaiah's own era of history, not in 1990.

In 1991 one writer argued that Iraq's invasion of Kuwait was a step toward the end-time Babylon of Isaiah 13. He said the 'day of the LORD' there is a future tribulation. The fulfilled reading sees three problems. First, the theory rests on a gap of nearly 2,000 years between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks. Second, Isaiah says the day of the LORD is 'near' (Isaiah 13:6). Third, Isaiah names the attackers: 'I will stir up the Medes against them' (13:17). Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC. Daniel records that Belshazzar was killed that night and Darius the Mede received the kingdom (Daniel 5:30-31). Babylon then slowly became a ruin, as Isaiah said (13:19-22).
Nabonidus Chronicle: Cyrus's army entered Babylon in October 539 BC.
Strabo (Geography 16.1.5), about the time of Christ, said Babylon was largely deserted.
Charles Dyer, 'The Rise of Babylon' (1991), proposed the Iraqi link.

Some futurists hold that Babylon never suffered the total, sudden destruction of Isaiah 13:19 and Jeremiah 50-51. So they expect a rebuilt literal Babylon to be destroyed in the future (compare Revelation 18). Others see a near fulfilment in 539 BC and a far fulfilment at the end. Many scholars see Isaiah's language as typical judgment poetry.
When Isaiah says 'the day of the LORD is near,' can 'near' mean thousands of years away?
On this reading, no. If 'near' does not mean close at hand, it means nothing. A literal reading should take the time word plainly.

This reading presses the literal method on its own users. Dispensational writers insist on reading Scripture plainly. Yet they read 'near' in Isaiah 13:6 as 2,500 years or more. Isaiah also says Babylon's 'days will not be prolonged' (13:22). The prophets often said a day of the LORD was near for their hearers. Obadiah said it was near for Edom (Obadiah 15). Ezekiel said it was near for Egypt (Ezekiel 30:3). Zephaniah said it was near for Judah (Zephaniah 1:7, 14). Each came within history. The same rule applies to the New Testament. When Revelation says 'the time is near' (Revelation 1:3; 22:10), it means near for its first readers.
Ezekiel 30:3-4: the day is near; a sword comes on Egypt. Nebuchadnezzar invaded Egypt about 568 BC.
Zephaniah 1:14: the great day is near and hastens. Jerusalem fell in 586 BC.
Compare Daniel 8:26 ('seal up the vision, for it refers to many days') with Revelation 22:10 ('do not seal... the time is near').

Futurists answer that 'near' can mean 'imminent' or 'next in God's plan'. They cite 2 Peter 3:8 ('a day is like a thousand years'). Others see a near historical fulfilment that also previews a final, far one. Some scholars say prophets often saw future events without time gaps, like mountain peaks.
Does 'the day of the LORD' always mean the final end of the world?
No. In the Old Testament it often means any time God comes in judgment on a nation, such as Babylon, Edom, Egypt or Judah.

On this reading, the day of the LORD is any day when God acts decisively in history. Isaiah used it for Babylon (Isaiah 13:6, 9) and for Edom (Isaiah 34:8). Ezekiel used it for Egypt (Ezekiel 30:2-4). Joel used it for a locust plague and invasion (Joel 1:15; 2:1). Amos used it for Israel's fall to Assyria (Amos 5:18-20). Zephaniah used it for Judah's fall to Babylon (Zephaniah 1:7-18). Each 'day' came in history. So it is a mistake to assume that every use points to one future tribulation period. A small correction: the book's link to 'the Lord's day' in Revelation 1:10 is weak. There John uses a different Greek phrase (kyriake hemera), which the early church used for Sunday.
Amos 5:18-20: 'darkness, not light'. Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC.
Isaiah 34:8-10: a day of vengeance on Edom, described as never-ending smoke.
Didache 14.1 (about AD 100) uses 'the Lord's day' for the day of Christian worship.

Most scholars agree the phrase has many historical uses. Futurists add that these past days preview a final Day of the LORD at Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10). Many see a pattern of near and far fulfilment. Some dispensationalists define the end-time Day of the LORD as including the tribulation and millennium.
How does Daniel's statue of four kingdoms help us understand Babylon's fall?
Daniel showed Babylon (gold) giving way to Medo-Persia (silver), Greece (bronze) and Rome (iron). God's stone kingdom then came and outlasts them all.

This reading uses Scripture to interpret Scripture. Nebuchadnezzar saw a statue of gold, silver, bronze and iron (Daniel 2:31-35). Daniel told him that he was the head of gold (2:38). Another kingdom would follow. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC (Daniel 5:28-31). Greece under Alexander defeated Persia in 331 BC. Rome took the eastern lands by 63 BC. 'In the days of those kings' God set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed (2:44). On this reading, that is Christ's kingdom, which came in the days of Rome (Mark 1:15). It defeats every rival kingdom (Psalms 2). So Babylon's prophecies are fulfilled. Modern states are not new versions of these ancient empires.
Daniel 5:28: 'Peres': your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.
Battle of Gaugamela, 331 BC: Alexander defeated Darius III.
Pompey entered Jerusalem in 63 BC, bringing Judea under Rome.

Most futurists agree on the four kingdoms. But they see the feet and ten toes as a future revived Roman Empire, crushed by the stone at Christ's second coming. Some critical scholars read the four as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece. Amillennialists generally agree with the reading given here.
Did Saddam Hussein's rebuilding of ancient Babylon fulfil prophecy?
On this reading, no. It was a nationalist project to attract tourists and honour Iraq's past. Copying the past does not fulfil prophecy.

From the 1980s Saddam Hussein rebuilt parts of Babylon. He put his own name on new bricks, as Nebuchadnezzar had done. Some prophecy writers saw this as the rise of end-time Babylon. Historian Edwin Yamauchi judged it as a matter of national pride and tourism, like the Shah of Iran's 1971 celebration at Persepolis. If any past glory inspired Saddam, it was the Abbasid caliphate of Baghdad (AD 750-1258). The fulfilled reading sees no prophetic link. If anything, Saddam's fall in 2003 illustrates a principle: rulers who exalt themselves like Babylon are brought low (Isaiah 14:12-15; Daniel 4:37). This is application, not fulfilment. Isaiah said Babylon would never be inhabited again as a great city (Isaiah 13:20).
Saddam's bricks bore the words 'built in the era of Saddam Hussein'.
In 2019 UNESCO listed Babylon as a World Heritage Site. It remains a ruin and tourist site, not a capital.
Daniel 4:30-37: Nebuchadnezzar boasted of 'great Babylon which I have built' and was humbled.

Some futurists still expect a literal rebuilt Babylon as a world economic center (Revelation 18). They saw Saddam's work as possible preparation and point to Zechariah 5:5-11 (the woman in the basket taken to Shinar). Others think Babylon in Revelation means a future world system, not the Iraqi site.
Was Saddam Hussein's 1990 invasion of Kuwait a step toward attacking Israel, as some prophecy writers said?
The facts point elsewhere. Iraq invaded Kuwait over oil, debts and border claims. It fired missiles at Israel only later, to break up the coalition against it.

John Walvoord said the invasion was a move to set up a base from which to attack Israel. This reading answers with the historical record. Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. The main motives were war debts, oil prices and old claims to Kuwaiti land. Iraq did not attack Israel until 18 January 1991, after the coalition began bombing. It fired Scud missiles from western Iraq, which is much closer to Israel than Kuwait is. The aim was to provoke Israel and split the Arab members of the coalition. Israel did not respond. So the events do not fit a prophetic plan in which Iraq moves to destroy Israel. Jesus warned against being led astray by rumours (Matthew 24:4-6).
About 40 Scud missiles struck Israel between January and February 1991.
Kuwait was liberated on 26-28 February 1991.
Iraq owed Kuwait billions of dollars from the Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988).

Futurist writers reply that Saddam's hostility to Israel was real and public, and that he paid families of attackers. They see the Gulf War as a 'preview' of end-time hostility from Babylon's region. Most now admit it was not the fulfilment some expected in 1991.
Who is 'Babylon the great' in Revelation 17-18?
Christians have named four main candidates: first-century Rome, a future revived Roman Empire, a rebuilt literal Babylon, or first-century Jerusalem. This reading argues for Jerusalem.

There are four common answers. Many scholars say Babylon is pagan Rome, the city on seven hills (Revelation 17:9). Futurists often say it is a future revived Rome or a world system. Some expect a literal rebuilt Babylon in Iraq. The fulfilled reading that this group follows says it is apostate Jerusalem of the first century. It begins with the time texts. Revelation says its events 'must soon take place' (1:1) and that 'the time is near' (1:3; 22:10). That rules out a distant future. It then compares Scripture with Scripture. Babylon is 'the great city' (14:8), and so is the city 'where their Lord was crucified' (11:8). The guilt for the blood of prophets (18:24) matches what Jesus said about Jerusalem (Matthew 23:34-37).
Revelation 11:8 and 16:19: 'the great city' is split into three parts.
1 Peter 5:13: 'she who is at Babylon' is often read as Rome, about AD 64.
Josephus, Jewish War 5.1.4: Jerusalem was divided into three warring factions during the siege.

Most commentators, including many preterists, identify Babylon with Rome: the seven hills, 'the kings of the earth' (17:18), and maritime trade (18:11-19). Futurists see a future city or system. Idealists see Babylon as the world's seductive power in every age. The Jerusalem view is held by a minority of scholars.
Why do Revelation's time statements matter for identifying Babylon?
Because John said repeatedly that his visions would 'soon' happen and that 'the time is near'. So Babylon must be a power of his own day.

On the fulfilled reading, Revelation itself sets the time frame. It opens by saying these things 'must soon take place' (1:1) and 'the time is near' (1:3). The risen Christ says 'I am coming quickly' several times (2:16; 3:11; 22:7, 12, 20). The book ends by repeating that the time is near (22:6, 10). John is told not to seal the book (22:10), unlike Daniel, who was told to seal his vision because it was far off (Daniel 8:26; 12:4). If Revelation was written before AD 70, then Babylon is a first-century power: Rome or Jerusalem. Without these time texts, the book can be made to fit any era, which is what many writers have done.
Revelation 22:10 compared with Daniel 12:4: one book sealed, the other open.
Many preterists date Revelation to about AD 65-68, during Nero's reign. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3) placed it late, near the end of Domitian's reign (about AD 95).

Futurists say 'soon' means suddenly or certainly. They also hold that most of the book is about the end. Most scholars date Revelation about AD 95 based on Irenaeus. For them, a Jerusalem identification is impossible, since the city had already fallen. Idealists say 'near' means each generation must be ready.
Why does the charge of shedding the blood of prophets point to Jerusalem?
Because Jesus laid the blood of all the prophets on Jerusalem and that generation. Revelation lays the same charge on Babylon.

Revelation says the harlot is drunk with the blood of the saints and of Jesus' witnesses (17:6). It also says that in her was found the blood of prophets and saints and of all who were slain on the earth (18:24). This reading compares Jesus' words in Matthew 23. He told the leaders of Jerusalem that all the righteous blood shed on earth, from Abel to Zechariah, would come on 'this generation' (Matthew 23:35-36). He added, 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets' (23:37). In Luke he said a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem (Luke 13:33). Stephen accused the council of killing those who foretold the Righteous One (Acts 7:51-52). Paul said the same (1 Thessalonians 2:14-16). The parallel is strong.
Matthew 23:35-36 and Revelation 18:24 both speak of 'all' the righteous blood shed on the earth.
Stephen was killed about AD 34 (Acts 7:58); James the brother of John about AD 44 (Acts 12:2).
Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1: James, the brother of Jesus, was stoned in Jerusalem in AD 62.

Those who see Rome reply that Rome also killed many saints. Nero's persecution in AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44) is a key example, and later emperors added more. They note that Revelation 17:6 speaks of 'martyrs of Jesus', suggesting imperial persecution. Futurists see an end-time persecution. The harsh words in these texts are about leaders in one generation, not the Jewish people as a whole.
Why would a 'harlot' fit unfaithful Jerusalem better than pagan Rome?
In the prophets, only a covenant wife can be called a harlot. God called Israel and Jerusalem a faithless wife many times. Rome was never God's bride.

On the fulfilled reading, the image of a harlot is covenant language. The prophets often pictured Israel's idolatry as adultery against God her husband. Ezekiel 16 tells the long story of Jerusalem as an unfaithful bride. Ezekiel 23 does the same for Samaria and Jerusalem. Isaiah says, 'How the faithful city has become a harlot!' (Isaiah 1:21). Jeremiah and Hosea use the same picture (Jeremiah 3:1-8; Hosea 2:2-5). A pagan city cannot break a marriage covenant it never had. Revelation also sets the harlot against the bride. The harlot falls, and the new Jerusalem comes down as a bride (Revelation 21:2). Paul contrasts 'the present Jerusalem', in slavery, with 'the Jerusalem above' (Galatians 4:25-26).
Isaiah 1:21: the faithful city has become a harlot.
Galatians 4:25-26: present Jerusalem in slavery; Jerusalem above is free.
Hebrews 12:22: believers have come to the heavenly Jerusalem.

Others note that the prophets also called pagan cities harlots. Nineveh is a harlot (Nahum 3:4) and Tyre is a forgotten harlot (Isaiah 23:15-17). So the image alone does not prove a covenant wife. They see the harlot as Rome's seductive trade and idolatry, or a world system in every age.
